answerSpec.modelAnswer: The victors' aims conflicted, so each had to compromise. Clemenceau wanted the Rhineland separated from Germany, but Wilson and Lloyd George refused, so it was only demilitarised and occupied; the leaders could not agree on a reparations figure, so it was left to a commission. Public opinion also limited what was possible: French and British voters demanded a harsh peace, so Wilson could not get the mild settlement he wanted. Finally, American politics undermined Wilson: his opponents in the Senate rejected the treaty, so the USA never joined the League and the promised Anglo-American guarantee to France lapsed, leaving France insecure.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There were strong reasons to justify the treaty in 1919. The war had been fought largely on French and Belgian soil, and France had lost about 1.3-1.4 million soldiers; most people in the Allied countries believed Germany had started the war. Germany had imposed the very harsh Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on Russia in 1918, which suggested how it would have treated the Allies. British and French voters demanded that Germany pay.

However, many at the time criticised it. Germany was not allowed to negotiate, so Germans called it a Diktat, and the war guilt clause placed all the blame on Germany. Self-determination was denied to Germans, who could not unite with Austria. In Britain Keynes argued that reparations would damage the whole European economy, while many in France thought the treaty too lenient to keep Germany weak.

Overall the treaty could be justified as a response to the war in the circumstances of 1919, but its manner and some of its terms were criticised even then, so I partly agree.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The main reason was that Germany fell behind with its reparations deliveries, such as coal and timber, at the end of 1922. France and Belgium decided to take what they were owed directly by occupying the Ruhr, Germany's main industrial region, in January 1923. France also wanted to show that the treaty would be enforced. It badly needed reparations to rebuild its devastated north-east and to repay war debts, and it felt insecure because the Anglo-American guarantee had lapsed, so it was determined to keep Germany weak.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The treaty caused many of Germany's problems. Because the new Republic's leaders signed it, nationalists called them the November criminals, and extremists murdered Erzberger in 1921 and Rathenau in 1922. The army cuts meant Freikorps units faced disbandment, and some backed the Kapp Putsch in March 1920. Reparations led to the occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923, and paying striking workers with printed money turned inflation into hyperinflation.

However, some problems had other causes. Germany had paid for the war by borrowing and printing money, so the mark was falling before 1919. Defeat and the revolution of 1918-1919 had already divided Germans, the Spartacist rising of January 1919 came before the treaty was signed, and the Weimar constitution's proportional representation produced weak coalitions. Hitler's Munich Putsch of November 1923 grew out of the crisis but also reflected right-wing hatred of democracy itself.

Overall the treaty was the most important single cause of Germany's problems to 1923, because it linked the Republic with humiliation and caused the Ruhr crisis, but it worked together with problems inherited from the war.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The League succeeded where the parties were small states willing to accept its authority. In the Aaland Islands dispute both Sweden and Finland asked the League to decide and accepted its ruling. Its decisions were sensible compromises: Finland kept the islands, but they were demilitarised and the islanders' Swedish language and culture were protected, so Sweden could accept the result. When Greece invaded Bulgaria in 1925, Britain and France backed the League's order to withdraw, and Greece, a small state, could not resist united great-power pressure, so it withdrew and paid compensation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The League had important successes in the 1920s. It settled the Aaland Islands dispute in 1921 and stopped Greece's invasion of Bulgaria in 1925. Its agencies did valuable work: Nansen organised the return of hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war and passports for refugees, the Health Organisation fought epidemics, the ILO pressed for better working conditions, and the 1926 Slavery Convention committed members to end slavery. It also arranged loans that rescued Austria and Hungary.

However, there were serious failures. Poland seized Vilna in 1920 and kept it, and in 1923 Mussolini occupied Corfu and forced Greece to pay compensation through the Conference of Ambassadors. Disarmament made no progress, and the most important agreements of the decade, Locarno and the Kellogg-Briand Pact, were made outside the League.

Overall the League was successful in humanitarian work and with small states, but the failures showed that it could not control a determined great power, so it was only partly successful.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The League's procedures were slow: China appealed in 1931, but the Lytton Commission did not report until October 1932, by which time Japan had set up Manchukuo. Britain and France, the League's leading members, were not prepared to impose sanctions that would hurt their own trade during the Depression or risk a war in Asia, where they had few forces. Economic sanctions would also have been weak because the USA, Japan's main trading partner, was not a member. When the Assembly accepted the Lytton Report, Japan simply left the League, and nothing more was done.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Depression was very important. It hit Japan's export trade hard and strengthened the army's case for seizing Manchuria; in Italy and Germany it encouraged leaders who promised greatness through expansion. It also made League members unwilling to impose sanctions that would cost them trade, and helped wreck the Disarmament Conference.

However, other factors were just as important. The League had weaknesses from the start: the USA was absent, it had no army and needed unanimity, so it was slow and its sanctions were full of gaps. Above all, Britain and France chose not to act firmly. Over Abyssinia they wanted to keep Mussolini as an ally against Hitler after the Stresa Front, so they left oil out of the sanctions, kept the Suez Canal open and drew up the Hoare-Laval Pact.

Overall the Depression created the crises, but it was the League's weaknesses and the choices of Britain and France that turned them into failures, so I only partly agree.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Abyssinian crisis was the turning point. Britain and France led the League in imposing sanctions on Italy in 1935, which angered Mussolini, while Germany did not join them. This ended the Stresa Front. answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Rhineland was a very important success. On 7 March 1936 Hitler broke both the Treaty of Versailles and the Locarno treaties by sending troops into the zone, and Britain and France did nothing. The gamble increased his confidence and his authority over doubtful generals, and Germany could now fortify its western border, which made it much harder for France to help its allies in eastern Europe.

However, other successes were also important. Rearmament and conscription, announced in 1935, gave Hitler the military strength that made all his later moves possible, and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement showed that Britain would accept breaches of Versailles, breaking the Stresa Front. The Saar plebiscite of 1935 was a popular, legal victory, and the Rome-Berlin Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact in 1936 gave Germany allies.

Overall rearmament was the foundation of Hitler's foreign policy, but the Rhineland was the most important single success because it showed that Britain and France would not use force, which encouraged everything that followed. I largely agree.

It was also a strategic threat: it had a well-equipped army, strong fortifications in the Sudeten mountains and alliances with France and the USSR, so it stood on Germany's flank. answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939 was very important to the timing of the war. It meant that Germany could attack Poland without fearing a war on two fronts, and its secret protocol divided Poland between Germany and the USSR. Hitler believed that without Soviet help Britain and France would not fight for Poland, and he invaded only nine days later.

However, the Pact was a short-term cause. Hitler's aim of Lebensraum in the east meant he would always seek to expand, and he had ordered plans for the invasion of Poland in April 1939, before the Pact. Appeasement had encouraged him to believe the West would back down, and the British and French guarantee to Poland in March 1939 meant that an attack on Poland was likely to mean war. The League's earlier failures had also shown that aggression went unpunished.

Overall the Pact was important because it made Hitler confident enough to attack when he did, but Hitler's aims were the main cause, so the Pact was a trigger rather than the root cause.

**Was the Treaty of Versailles fair?** Study the sources and answer all parts.

**Source A** — a cartoon of the kind published in a British magazine in May 1919, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> Three well-dressed gentlemen, labelled "France", "Britain" and "America", stand around a table on which lies a large map of Germany. France is cutting off pieces with a large pair of scissors. Britain is quietly pocketing a handful of small flags marked "Colonies". America stands a little apart, holding a book titled "Fourteen Points" and looking uncomfortable. A thin German figure watches through a window, kept out by a locked door.

**Source B** — an editorial in a German newspaper, June 1919 (newspaper and writer fictional) (invented for this question)

> Today the German people must sign their own humiliation. We are told that we alone caused the war, though every nation armed and every nation mobilised. We are robbed of our colonies, our coal and our sons' right to defend their homeland. This is not a peace of justice, as President Wilson promised, but a peace of vengeance.

**Source C** — an editorial in a French newspaper, June 1919 (newspaper and writer fictional) (invented for this question)

> Germany keeps its industry, its railways and sixty million people, while our northern provinces lie in ruins. Our soldiers stand on the Rhine for only fifteen years. Who believes that a nation which has attacked us twice in fifty years will be content? The treaty is too weak to protect France.

**Source D** — a letter from a fictional British economist to a London newspaper, December 1919 (invented for this question)

> I do not ask readers to pity Germany. I ask them to think of their own pockets. If Germany must spend every mark on reparations, it cannot buy our cotton, our coal or our machines. A Europe in which the largest economy is crippled will be a Europe in which British workers are unemployed.

**Source E** — a speech by a fictional British Member of Parliament in the House of Commons, July 1919 (invented for this question)

> The treaty is stern, but it is just. Germany chose war in 1914 and must bear the cost. Belgium was invaded, France ravaged, and our ships sunk without warning. Those who now plead for Germany forget the peace it forced upon Russia only last year.

**Source F** — a cartoon of the kind published in an American newspaper in 1919, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A small, ragged figure labelled "Germany" stands in front of a towering pile of papers labelled "Bill for damages" that reaches into the clouds. A banker in a top hat, labelled "Allied Reparations Commission", hands him a pen. In the background, a thin factory chimney gives off only a wisp of smoke.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The letter was written to persuade British readers that heavy reparations were against Britain's own interests. The writer avoids asking for pity for Germany and instead appeals to readers' pockets: if Germany spends everything on reparations it cannot buy British cotton, coal and machines, and British workers will lose their jobs. It was written in December 1919 because reparations were being hotly debated: the total had not yet been fixed (it was set in 1921), Britain faced economic difficulties after the war, and the economist Keynes had just published a similar argument. answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source D is useful because it shows one important reason for appeasement: Britain was not ready for war in 1938. The official has seen the figures and says there were too few modern fighters and the radar stations were unfinished, so bombers could have reached London. This matches my knowledge that British military chiefs warned Chamberlain that air defences were not ready. As a private diary written by someone with access to official figures, it has no reason to mislead. However, he is a junior official and writes only about air defence; the source says nothing about other reasons, such as public fear of war, the unwillingness of the Dominions to fight, or the belief that the Sudeten Germans had a fair claim. It is useful, but only for part of the explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source E supports the critics of Munich. An eyewitness American journalist reports German troops entering Prague in March 1939, a city with almost no Germans, which proved that Hitler's claim to want only his own people was false. Source F, however, supports the defenders of Munich: by August 1939 the pilot's squadron had new fighters and was at full strength, whereas a year earlier its aircraft were obsolete. This fits my knowledge that Britain used the year after Munich to build fighters and radar stations, though Germany also rearmed. E is reliable on events, being an eyewitness report from a neutral country; F is one pilot's private view but matches what we know. Together they show that the critics were right that Hitler could not be trusted, but that the year gained was not wasted.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Some sources suggest that Munich was a mistake. Source A predicts that Hitler would demand ever more, Source B describes the betrayal of Czechoslovakia, which lost its fortresses and factories, and Source E shows that within six months Hitler had taken Prague, breaking his word. E is especially convincing because it is an eyewitness report of what actually happened; B is understandably bitter, being Czech.

Other sources defend Munich. Source C shows the relief of the British public and the belief that the Sudeten Germans deserved self-determination, though it was written on the day after Munich, before Prague. Source D shows Britain was not ready for war in 1938, and Source F shows that a year later the RAF was much stronger. D and F are private writings by people in a position to know, so they are fairly convincing about British weakness and the time gained.

Overall the sources convincingly show that Munich was a moral and political mistake, because Hitler could not be satisfied, but they also show that in military terms the time gained helped Britain. On balance they suggest it was a mistake, but an understandable one.

stem:
**Why did the League fail to stop Italy in Abyssinia?** Study the sources and answer all parts.

**Source A** — a cartoon of the kind published in a British magazine in late 1935, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A small, dignified African figure labelled "Abyssinia" stands at the door of a grand building marked "League of Nations". Inside, two plump gentlemen labelled "Britain" and "France" are seated at a table with a Roman soldier labelled "Italy", sharing a large map. One of the gentlemen calls over his shoulder to the doorway: "We shall consider your case presently."

**Source B** — an editorial in an Italian newspaper, October 1935 (newspaper and writer fictional) (invented for this question)

> Italy brings roads, schools and order to a land of slavery and chaos. Britain and France built their empires with the sword and now preach to us about the Covenant. Let them close their own colonies before they close their markets to Italian goods. Italy will not be stopped by a league of hypocrites.

**Source C** — a letter from a fictional Ethiopian student in London to a British newspaper, May 1936 (invented for this question)

> My country trusted the Covenant. We bought no great armies because we believed that the League would protect its members. Your sanctions stopped Italian cheese and hats, but not the oil that fuelled the aeroplanes that sprayed gas on our villages. Tell me, sir, who will trust the League now?

**Source D** — an editorial in a British newspaper, December 1935 (newspaper and writer fictional) (invented for this question)

> The plan agreed in Paris would hand Mussolini great stretches of Abyssinia as a reward for his aggression. It is a betrayal of everything this country promised at Geneva only weeks ago. The government must withdraw it at once, and the Foreign Secretary must go.

**Source E** — an editorial in a French newspaper, September 1935 (newspaper and writer fictional) (invented for this question)

> France has one enemy in Europe, and he sits in Berlin. In April at Stresa we gained a friend in Rome who has stood with us on the Brenner. Shall we throw away that friendship for the sake of a distant African empire? Prudence, not sentiment, must guide French policy.

**Source F** — a report by a fictional Swiss journalist in Geneva, July 1936 (invented for this question)

> Today the Assembly voted to end sanctions against Italy. Few delegates looked up from their papers. Abyssinia has fallen, its emperor is in exile, and the great experiment of collective security has ended not with a bang but with a shrug. The small nations have drawn their own conclusions.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: At a simple level, the cartoon shows Abyssinia left waiting at the League's door while its case is put off. The deeper message is that Britain and France, who controlled the League, were dealing with Italy behind Abyssinia's back: they sit at the table sharing a map with the Roman soldier, while the victim is told it will be considered "presently". This fits my knowledge: after the Walwal incident Haile Selassie's appeals were delayed, Britain and France wanted to keep Mussolini as an ally after the Stresa Front, and in December 1935 the Hoare-Laval Pact proposed giving Italy much of Abyssinia. The cartoonist is accusing the great powers of betraying the League.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources disagree about the invasion itself. Source B, from an Italian newspaper, presents it as a civilising mission bringing roads and schools, and says Britain and France are hypocrites with empires of their own. Source C, by an Ethiopian student, presents Abyssinia as a peaceful member betrayed by the League and attacked with aircraft and gas. They also disagree about sanctions: B treats them as an outrage, while C says they were too weak because oil was not included. Yet they agree on one thing: both suggest that the League's stand lacked credibility, B because its leaders were hypocrites and C because no one would trust it again. Overall they disagree deeply, but both undermine the League.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The editorial was published because the Hoare-Laval Pact had just been leaked in December 1935. The plan, agreed in Paris by the British and French foreign ministers, would have given Italy a large part of Abyssinia. The writer's purpose was to express public outrage and put pressure on the government: he calls the plan a reward for aggression and a betrayal of promises made at Geneva, and demands that it be withdrawn and the Foreign Secretary dismissed. This worked: in the face of public anger the plan was dropped and Samuel Hoare resigned. It reflects the strong support for the League among British voters at that time.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source E helps to explain the outcome in Source F. The French editorial shows that France saw Germany as its real enemy and valued Italy as an ally after the Stresa Front, so it was unwilling to risk that friendship for Abyssinia. This explains why sanctions were weak and why, as Source F reports, the Assembly ended them in July 1936 with little concern. However, E gives only the French view. My knowledge shows other reasons: Britain too wanted to keep Italy friendly, oil was not banned partly because the USA was not a member, the Suez Canal stayed open, and the war ended in only seven months. E explains an important part of the outcome but not all of it.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Several sources blame Britain and France. Source A shows them dealing with Italy behind the League's back, Source D shows the British public's anger at the Hoare-Laval Pact, which rewarded aggression, and Source E reveals that France put its friendship with Italy against Germany before Abyssinia. Source C adds that sanctions excluded oil, a decision Britain and France could have changed. These are fairly convincing because D and E come from British and French newspapers themselves.

Other sources suggest wider causes. Source B shows that Mussolini was determined to conquer regardless of sanctions, and turns the charge of hypocrisy against colonial powers. Source F, from a neutral Swiss journalist, describes a general collapse of will among all members, not just Britain and France. My knowledge adds that the USA was not a member and the Depression made members reluctant to lose trade.

Overall the sources provide convincing evidence that Britain and France were mainly responsible, since they led the League and chose not to act firmly, but they also show that the League's wider weaknesses and Italy's determination played a part.
